title: The Machine That Is You
subtitle: Heart, blood, bones, brain and the army that keeps you well
subject: Body

pages.h: The machine that never switches off
p: You are a machine made of about 30 trillion tiny parts called cells. That is 30 followed by 12 zeros, nearly 4,000 times more parts than there are people on Earth. Your machine runs day and night. It never stops for repairs. It fixes itself while it works, keeps itself at about 37 degrees Celsius and grows bigger every year.

A car has about 30,000 parts and needs a mechanic. Your body builds new parts, replaces worn ones and fights off invaders without you ever thinking about it. This book is a tour of the most amazing machine you will ever own. It is the one you are sitting in right now.
pages.cap: Every cell is a tiny living factory with its own power plants and instruction book.
pages.fact: Did you know? Most of your cells are smaller than a tenth of a millimetre. Several could line up across the width of a hair.

p: Cells are the bricks your body is built from, but they are bricks that are alive. There are about 200 kinds. Skin cells are flat like tiles. Muscle cells are long like ropes. Nerve cells have branches like trees. Red blood cells look like tiny dented doughnuts.

Inside almost every cell is a curled-up instruction book called DNA. Stretched out, the DNA from one cell would be about 2 metres long, yet it folds into a space far smaller than a speck of dust. It tells each cell what to build and when to make a copy of itself. Your skin cells are replaced every 2 to 4 weeks. The outer you is always new.
pages.cap: DNA is a twisted ladder of code. Almost every cell in your body carries a full copy.

p: Make a fist. That is about the size of your heart. It is a muscle with four rooms, and it is really two pumps side by side. The right side pushes blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side pushes that fresh blood to the rest of you. Both halves squeeze at the same moment. That squeeze is a heartbeat.

A child's heart beats about 90 times a minute, around 130,000 times a day. It pumps about 4 litres of blood every minute, enough to fill a bathtub in about half an hour. Over a long life it will beat more than 3 billion times without ever taking a day off. No machine built by people has come close.
pages.cap: Blood low on oxygen comes in on the right, goes to the lungs, and leaves the left side rich in oxygen.
pages.fact: Did you know? The thump-thump you hear is not the squeeze. It is the sound of the heart's little doors snapping shut.

p: Blood is a river of deliveries. A nine-year-old has about 2.5 litres of it. More than half is a watery liquid called plasma. Floating in it are more than 10 trillion red blood cells. Each one carries oxygen from your lungs to every other cell, then carries away carbon dioxide waste. Blood is red because red cells are full of iron, and iron turns red when oxygen sticks to it, like rust.

Blood travels through tubes called vessels. The biggest is as thick as a garden hose. The smallest are thinner than a hair. Laid end to end, your vessels would stretch about 100,000 kilometres, enough to wrap around the Earth twice. A single red cell makes the whole round trip in about one minute.
pages.cap: Your blood vessels, laid end to end, would circle the Earth more than twice.
pages.fact: Did you know? Your bone marrow makes about 2 million new red blood cells every second to replace old ones.

pages.q: About how many times does a child's heart beat in one day?
pages.why: Around 90 beats a minute times 60 minutes times 24 hours is about 130,000 beats. Your heart does that every single day.

p: Every heartbeat sends a wave down your arteries. You can feel it.
steps: Turn one hand palm up. Press two fingers of the other hand gently on the wrist, just below the thumb, until you feel a soft tapping.
Count the taps for 30 seconds and double the number. That is your resting heart rate.
Do 30 jumping jacks, then count again right away. How much faster is it?
Sit quietly and count once a minute. How long does your heart take to calm back down?
pages.cap: Count for 30 seconds, then double it.
pages.safe: Use your fingers, not your thumb. Your thumb has a pulse of its own.

pages.h: Lungs: two sponges full of air
p: You take about 20,000 breaths a day and hardly notice one. Each breath pulls air down your windpipe into two spongy lungs. Inside, the pipes split into smaller and smaller branches, like an upside-down tree. At the tips are about 300 million tiny air bags called alveoli. Spread flat, they would cover around 70 square metres, the size of a badminton court.

Why so much surface? Oxygen has to pass through the thin walls of these bags into your blood, and carbon dioxide has to pass out. More surface means a faster swap. A sheet of muscle under your lungs, the diaphragm, pulls down to suck air in and relaxes to push it out. Hiccups are the diaphragm twitching.
pages.cap: Air goes in, oxygen crosses into the blood, and carbon dioxide comes back out.
pages.fact: Did you know? The air you breathe in is 21 percent oxygen. The air you breathe out still has 16 percent. Your body uses only a quarter of it.

pages.h: Why you puff when you run
p: Your muscles burn food and oxygen to make energy, the way a fire burns wood and air. When you run, your muscles need up to 15 times more oxygen than when you sit. Your body has sensors that notice carbon dioxide building up in your blood. They tell your brain, and your brain tells your lungs and heart to speed up.

Sitting still, you breathe about 20 times a minute and your heart beats about 90 times. In a hard sprint you might breathe 60 times a minute while your heart races at nearly 200. After you stop, you keep puffing for a while. Your body is paying back the oxygen it borrowed.
pages.cap: The harder you work, the faster your heart pumps oxygen to your muscles.

pages.h: Your lungs have enough surface to cover a badminton court
p: About 300 million tiny air bags, folded into a space the size of two footballs. That is how your blood grabs oxygen fast enough to keep you alive.

pages.h: Bones: the frame that is alive
p: An adult has 206 bones. A baby has about 300. Many of them join together as you grow, which is why you have fewer bones now than when you were born. Your biggest bone is the femur in your thigh. Your smallest is in your ear and is only 3 millimetres long, smaller than a grain of rice.

Bones are not dry sticks. They are alive, with blood vessels and nerves. Weight for weight, bone is about four times stronger than concrete. Inside the big bones is a soft jelly called marrow, where your blood cells are made. Bones slowly rebuild themselves too. Over about 10 years, your skeleton is almost completely replaced.
pages.cap: Your skeleton holds you up, protects your organs and makes your blood.
pages.fact: Did you know? More than half of your bones are in your hands and feet: 27 in each hand and 26 in each foot.

p: Bones cannot bend. You can because of joints, the places where two bones meet. Your knee and elbow are hinge joints, like a door. They swing one way. Your shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints. A round bone end sits in a cup and can swing in every direction. That is why you can windmill your arm but not your knee.

Why do bones not grind each other to dust? Their ends are capped with cartilage, a smooth rubbery layer, and bathed in slippery fluid. It is slicker than ice on ice. Strong straps called ligaments tie the bones together. That popping sound when you crack your knuckles is a gas bubble in the fluid, not the bone.
pages.cap: Joints let bones move against each other smoothly, like well-oiled parts in a machine.

pages.q: How many bones does an adult have?
pages.why: Adults have 206 bones. Babies start with about 300 smaller bones, and many of them fuse together as a child grows.

p: You have about 600 muscles, and together they make up about a third of your weight. Every one works the same way: it can only shorten and pull. A muscle cannot push. So how do you straighten your arm? Muscles work in pairs. The biceps on the front pulls your forearm up. The triceps on the back pulls it straight again. While one pulls, the other relaxes.

Muscles attach to bones with tough cords called tendons. Your arm is a lever. The elbow is the turning point, the biceps pulls near it, and your hand swings far out at the end. It takes a strong pull near the elbow to lift a small weight in your hand. That is why your biceps is so thick.
pages.cap: Your arm is a lever. The muscle pulls close to the hinge to move the hand far away.
pages.fact: Did you know? It takes about 12 muscles to smile and 11 to frown. The old saying that frowning takes more is a myth.

p: You choose to move your arms and legs. But your heart beats, your stomach churns and your blood vessels squeeze without any order from you. These are involuntary muscles. The heart is made of a special muscle found nowhere else. Smooth muscle lines your gut and pushes food along in slow waves, even when you are asleep.

Muscles also make heat. When you are cold, your brain makes them twitch rapidly. That is shivering, and it can double the heat your body makes. The hardest-working muscles are around your eyes, which move about 100,000 times a day. The strongest for its size is the one in your jaw. It can bite with a force of about 70 kilograms.
pages.cap: Shivering is hundreds of muscles twitching at once to warm you up.

pages.h: Try it: the tired muscle test
p: Find out what happens when a muscle runs low on fuel.
steps: Hold a clothes peg between your thumb and first finger. Open and close it as fast as you can for 20 seconds while a friend counts.
Without resting, keep going for another 20 seconds. Count again. Then do a third 20 seconds.
Compare the three numbers. Most people get slower each time because waste builds up in the muscle faster than blood can carry it away.
Rest for two minutes and try once more. Does the number bounce back?
pages.cap: Tendons run over bones like ropes over pulleys, turning a muscle pull into finger movement.

p: Your brain weighs about 1.3 kilograms, a bit more than a bag of sugar. It is pinkish-grey, soft like tofu and about three quarters water. It sits in total darkness inside your skull, yet it sees, hears, remembers, imagines and runs your whole body at once. It contains about 86 billion nerve cells with trillions of connections between them.

The brain is only 2 percent of your weight, but it uses 20 percent of your energy. It is working hard even when you sleep, sorting the day's memories. Children aged 9 need about 10 hours of sleep a night for this. Strangely, the brain itself cannot feel pain. It has no pain sensors of its own.
pages.cap: Nerve cells pass signals to each other across tiny gaps, billions of times every second.
pages.fact: Did you know? By age 9 your brain is already about 95 percent of its adult size. The rest of you has a lot of catching up to do.

pages.h: Nerves: wires faster than a race car
p: Your brain talks to your body through nerves, long thin cells that carry signals as tiny electric pulses. The fastest nerves send a message at about 120 metres per second, around 430 kilometres per hour. A message from your brain to your toes takes about one hundredth of a second. A thick cable of nerves, the spinal cord, runs down inside your backbone like a main road.

Some things are too urgent to wait for the brain. Touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you feel the burn. The signal goes to your spinal cord, which fires an order straight back to your arm. The pain message reaches your brain a moment later. That shortcut is called a reflex.
pages.cap: Nerves carry signals like wires carry electricity, using tiny pulses and chemical messengers.
pages.fact: Did you know? The nerve from your spine to your big toe is a single cell about a metre long.

pages.q: You touch something hot and your hand jerks back before you feel pain. Why?
opts: Your hand has its own tiny brain
The spinal cord sends the order without waiting for the brain
pages.why: This is a reflex. The signal from your hand reaches the spinal cord, which fires an order straight back to the arm muscles. The brain finds out a moment later.

p: Your senses are the body's way of collecting news. Your eyes can tell apart about 10 million colours. Your ears hold about 15,000 tiny hairs that wobble when sound arrives, and each wobble becomes a nerve signal. Your tongue has roughly 10,000 taste buds, and every one of them is replaced about every two weeks.

You have more than five senses. You can feel heat, cold, pain and pressure. You know where your arms are with your eyes shut. A sense organ in your inner ear tells you which way is up, which is why spinning makes you dizzy. Your nose is the champion. Scientists think it can tell apart more than a trillion smells, though they still argue about the exact number.
pages.cap: Sound waves wobble tiny hairs deep in your ear, and each wobble becomes a message to the brain.

p: Your digestive system is one long tube that runs from your mouth to the other end. Stretched out, it would be about 9 metres long, more than six times your height. Food goes in one end, the useful parts are pulled out along the way, and the leftovers come out the other end.

The work starts before you swallow. Your mouth makes about 1 litre of saliva a day, and it begins breaking down food the moment you chew. A nine-year-old has a mix of baby teeth and new adult teeth, heading for 32. When you swallow, muscles in your food pipe squeeze the lump down in about 8 seconds. They push so well that you could swallow standing on your head.
pages.cap: Saliva starts dissolving food the moment it touches your tongue.
pages.fact: Did you know? Astronauts eat upside down all the time. Muscles, not gravity, move your food.

p: Your stomach is a muscular bag that churns food for 2 to 4 hours in acid strong enough to dissolve metal. Why does it not digest itself? Its walls are coated in thick slime, and the lining is replaced every 3 or 4 days. The mushy result flows into the small intestine, a 6 metre tube folded up inside you.

The small intestine is lined with millions of tiny fingers called villi. They soak up sugars, fats and proteins into your blood. Flattened out, the surface would cover about 30 square metres. Your liver, the body's chemical factory, does more than 500 jobs with what arrives. The large intestine takes back water from what is left. The whole trip takes one to two days.

v.title: A meal's journey
items: Soaked up in the small intestine

pages.cap: A meal takes a day or two to travel from your mouth to the other end.

pages.h: Your stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal
p: It is strong enough to burn your skin. Only a thick coat of slime, renewed every few days, stops your stomach from digesting itself.

pages.q: Why does your stomach not digest itself?
opts: Its acid is actually very weak
It is lined with thick slime and rebuilds its lining every few days
It only works when food is inside
pages.why: Stomach acid is strong, but a layer of mucus protects the walls, and the cells of the lining are replaced every 3 or 4 days before damage can build up.

p: Germs are living things too small to see. A bacterium is about one thousandth of a millimetre long. A thousand could sit side by side on the dot of this i. Viruses are 100 times smaller still. They cannot even live on their own. They have to break into one of your cells and make it build copies of them. That is what a cold does to your nose.

Most bacteria are not enemies. Your gut is home to about 38 trillion of them, more than you have human cells, and they help digest your food. The problem is the few that make you sick. A sneeze fires about 40,000 droplets at 100 kilometres per hour, and each droplet can carry thousands of germs.
pages.cap: Bacteria and viruses are tiny, but your white blood cells can hunt them down.
pages.fact: Did you know? Washing your hands with soap for 20 seconds, about two rounds of the alphabet, removes most germs.

p: Your body defends itself like a castle. The outer wall is your skin, and almost nothing gets through unbroken skin. The gates, your nose and mouth, are guarded by sticky mucus that traps invaders and by acid in your stomach that destroys them. Tears and saliva carry chemicals that kill germs on contact.

If invaders get inside, the soldiers come out. White blood cells patrol your blood and swallow germs whole. Some make antibodies, little tags that stick to one kind of germ and mark it for destruction. Fever is a weapon too. Raising your temperature from 37 to 39 degrees slows the germs down and speeds up your soldiers. Pus in a cut is a pile of white blood cells that fought and won.
pages.cap: Skin is the wall, mucus and acid guard the gates, and white blood cells are the soldiers inside.
pages.fact: Did you know? Only about 1 percent of your blood cells are white, but one drop of blood holds more than 300,000 of them.

p: Once your white blood cells have beaten a germ, some of them remember it for years. If the same germ returns, they attack at once, before you even feel ill. That is why you catch chickenpox only once. A vaccine uses this trick. It shows your body a harmless piece or copy of a germ, so your defenders learn the enemy without you ever being sick.

The first vaccine was made in 1796 by an English doctor named Edward Jenner, against smallpox. In the 1900s alone smallpox killed about 300 million people. After a worldwide vaccination campaign it was wiped out in 1980. It is the only human disease ever to be completely erased.

v.title: When most people are protected, germs run out of places to go

pages.cap: When most people in a group are vaccinated, germs cannot spread far, which protects the few who cannot be vaccinated.

p: At age 9 you grow about 5 or 6 centimetres a year, mostly while you sleep. Near the ends of your long bones are soft growth plates where new bone is added. A chemical released at night tells them to build. During the teenage years growth speeds up, then the plates harden and growing stops.

Your body is also always mending. Cut your finger and platelets in your blood rush to the hole and stick together to form a plug within minutes. The plug dries into a scab, a shield while new skin grows underneath. A broken bone knits back together in about 6 to 8 weeks. Your skin sheds about 30,000 dead cells every minute, and new ones take their place.
pages.cap: You grow in spurts, fastest as a baby and again as a teenager, and your body is always repairing itself.
pages.fact: Did you know? You are about 1 centimetre taller in the morning than at night. Gravity squashes the pads between your backbones during the day.

qs: Your body replaces most of its cells over the years. Are you still the same person you were at age 3? What makes you you?
If you could give your body one upgrade, like faster nerves or stronger bones, what would you choose and what might go wrong?
